source_metadata.title: From Plan to Action: How Well Do Agents Follow the Plan?
source_metadata.source_type: empirical software-engineering study / ASE 2026 conference paper; arXiv v3 preprint
source_metadata.conference: 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated how well programming agents follow instructed task plans and how plan compliance relates to issue-resolution success.
The primary evaluation used 497 SWE-bench Verified instances after excluding three Very Hard instances that no studied model resolved under any plan setting.

population.label: 497 SWE-bench Verified instances spanning Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty

atoms.canonical_statement: The generalization evaluation used 266 Python instances from SWE-bench Pro.

population.label: 266 Python SWE-bench Pro instances used for generalization experiments

atoms.canonical_statement: Experiments used the SWE-agent scaffold with GPT-5 mini, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, and Devstral-small as backbone language models.
The Standard program-repair plan consisted of Navigation, Reproduction, Patch, and Validation in that order.
The study evaluated eight plan settings: Standard, No Plan, No Reproduction, No Validation, added regression testing, added summary, reordered phases, and periodic plan reminders.
The periodic-reminder setting re-injected the Standard plan every five trajectory steps.

Raw agent actions were mapped to plan phases using file/directory inspection for Navigation, generated pre-patch tests for Reproduction, application-code edits for Patch, and generated post-patch tests for Validation; existing repository tests were treated as regression testing outside the default plan.
Plan Phase Compliance (PPC) measured the fraction of instructed plan phases that appeared at least once in a trajectory.
Plan Order Compliance (POC) measured the fraction of instructed phases whose first occurrences formed the expected relative order using the longest increasing subsequence.
Plan Phase Fidelity (PPF) penalized phases appearing in a trajectory that were outside the instructed plan alphabet.
Overall Plan Compliance (PC) was defined as the geometric mean of PPC, POC, and PPF.
The evaluation additionally reported issue-resolution success rate, Graphectory node/edge/loop counts, and phase-flow Sankey analyses.
Two authors independently annotated 320 sampled actions for mapping validation, and agreement among the two human annotations and automated labels had Fleiss kappa of 0.99.
Under the Standard plan on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-5 mini achieved an issue-resolution success rate of 56.3%.

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard-plan compliance varied across models: Devstral-small most consistently covered phases in order, GPT-5 mini adapted by problem difficulty, DeepSeek-V3 had near-perfect phase fidelity but lower phase/order coverage, and DeepSeek-R1 had the lowest compliance.

Resolved trajectories had significantly higher plan compliance for Devstral-small (p=1e-5) and DeepSeek-R1 (p=0.032); the association was not statistically significant for DeepSeek-V3 (p=0.60) or GPT-5 mini (p=0.285).
GPT-5 mini often skipped Reproduction on easier problems but followed the instructed Standard plan more closely as problem difficulty increased.
Average Graphectory node/edge/loop counts were approximately 86/179/64 for Devstral-small, 38/49/18 for GPT-5 mini, 15/27/4 for DeepSeek-V3, and 14/21/4 for DeepSeek-R1.

atoms.canonical_statement: Pearson correlations between overall plan compliance and Graphectory complexity metrics were very weak positive correlations, with 0 < r <= 0.2.
The authors considered the Standard plan incomplete because GPT-5 mini and Devstral-small frequently ran existing repository tests in addition to the plan-prescribed generated tests.
Without an explicit plan, Devstral-small still largely followed N-R-P-V, GPT-5 mini often followed a subset without Reproduction, and the DeepSeek models largely reduced trajectories to N-P patterns.
Removing the Standard plan reduced success across all four models, with the largest performance loss observed in the DeepSeek models and particularly DeepSeek-R1.
In the No Plan setting, DeepSeek-V3 resolved 23 SWE-bench Verified instances that it did not resolve under the Standard plan.

atoms.canonical_statement: Manual inspection linked many No Plan-only resolutions to failed or incorrect reproduction-test generation under the Standard plan, after which the No Plan trajectory skipped reproduction and generated the correct patch.

atoms.canonical_statement: Adding regression-test execution caused only small success changes for Devstral-small and GPT-5 mini, but DeepSeek-V3 had a larger performance drop and low PPC, consistent with difficulty incorporating the added phases.
Under the regression-testing plan, Devstral-small tended to run regression tests after Navigation and after Validation, while GPT-5 mini tended to run them first and again after Validation.
With the added Summary phase, DeepSeek-R1 exhibited pervasive tool-calling failures in 413 instances.

population.label: 497 SWE-bench Verified instances spanning Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty

atoms.canonical_statement: Adding a final change-summary phase produced minimal behavioral and success-rate changes for Devstral-small, GPT-5 mini, and DeepSeek-V3 because the phase generally occurred after the core repair process.
The authors concluded that plan augmentation is useful only when aligned with a model's internal strategy and can degrade performance when added phases are not naturally employed by the model.
Under the reordered N-P-R-V plan, DeepSeek-V3 resolved 196 instances versus 191 under the Standard plan in the initial comparison.

population.label: 497 SWE-bench Verified instances spanning Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty

quantitative_result.effect_measure: resolved instance count under reordered plan

atoms.canonical_statement: Devstral-small often performed Reproduction before Patch despite the reordered N-P-R-V instruction, indicating preference for its established reproduction-first workflow.
The authors concluded that agents prioritize effective workflows over prescribed phase ordering when the instructed order conflicts with their problem-solving process.
After accounting for nondeterminism, the reordered plan changed DeepSeek-V3 success rate only negligibly, from 38.3% to 38.0%.

population.label: 497 SWE-bench Verified instances spanning Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty

atoms.canonical_statement: Periodic plan reminders improved plan compliance for DeepSeek-V3, maintained similar overall PC for the other models, and produced consistent success improvements across models.
For more meaningful SWE-bench Pro comparisons, the analysis retained 31 Python instances that at least one studied LLM could resolve under the Standard plan.

atoms.canonical_statement: On SWE-bench Pro, agents spent more effort in repetitive Navigation and Patching without reaching Validation, while most agents still skipped Reproduction.
To assess nondeterminism, the Standard-plan experiments were repeated three times and compared with pairwise McNemar tests.
Pairwise McNemar tests found statistically significant differences across Standard-plan runs, confirming nondeterminism in agent outcomes.
The reproducible subset with outcomes consistent across Standard-plan repeats contained 401 instances for GPT-5 mini.

atoms.canonical_statement: On reproducible subsets, the main conclusions persisted: plan reduction, augmentation, and reordering affected models differently according to their underlying strategy, and periodic reminders consistently improved performance.
The study evaluated only four language models, two software-engineering benchmarks, and a phase-level abstraction that may omit fine-grained or project-specific actions.
The authors identified possible data contamination and workflow overfitting on SWE-bench Verified as threats to interpreting plan compliance as genuine plan-following ability.
The authors argued that plan compliance should be used as a process-level signal rather than a maximized objective, because strict compliance is not always necessary or beneficial.

source_anchor.paragraph: Implications for Agent Design and Training

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors proposed using compliance signals for online monitoring, targeted reminders, adaptive plan refinement, and process-level post-training supervision while preserving agent flexibility.

source_anchor.paragraph: Implications for Agent Design and Training

atoms.canonical_statement: The paper concluded that plans materially affect issue-resolution success, but agents often struggle to comply with them, leaving room for improved plans and improved plan-following.
The paper states that its artifacts are publicly available through the cited artifact website.
The work reports support from NSF CCF-2238045 and IBM-Illinois Discovery Accelerator Institute grants.

extraction_limitations: Atoms were extracted from the 12-page article and its rendered main-text figures/tables; the external artifact repository and supplementary implementation files were not inspected because @ATOM did not request external verification.
Figure-based values were normalized from the rendered article into structured quantitative-result fields; narrative interpretations remain separate atoms.

The paper reports several possible causal explanations for plan violations (for example data contamination, context-window pressure, and short-term reward optimization); where these were speculative, they were not converted into directly reported causal results.
No conflict-of-interest statement was located in the supplied article text; therefore no conflict_of_interest atom was created.
